Even if we conclude that these references do support the existence of some 
limit, one might argue that does not end the debate on whether we today 
should maintain the status quo or toughen the nondelegation doctrine to strike 
down acts that have previously been upheld. Recall Coglianese’s interpretation 
of the status quo: that the NIRA provision invalidated in Schechter Poultry is 
more extreme than all the other delegations in the case law, such that 
Schechter remains good law. If we accept that interpretation, then originalist 
evidence for some unspecified limit on delegation may not justify rejecting our 
current doctrine, because that doctrine already provides some limit.
Some advocates for toughening the doctrine have countered this thinking 
by arguing that originahst sources support a version of the doctrine that is 
hard-edged and clearly tougher than what we have—^in particular, that 
rulemaking is categorically unconstitutional. E.g., Dep’t of Transportation v. 
Association of American Railroads, 575 U.S. 43, 66-91 (2015) (Thomas, J., 
concurring in the judgment); Phihp Hamburger, Is Administrative Law 
Unlawful? 83—110 (2014); PhUip Hamburger, Nondelegation Blues, 91 Geo. 
Wash. L. Rev. 1083 (2023); Aaron Gordon, Nondelegation Misinformation: A 
Reply to the Skeptics, 75 Baylor L. Rev. 152 (2023); Michael B. Rappaport, A 
Two-Tiered and Categorical Approach to the Nondelegation Doctrine, in THE

What of early practice under the Constitution? Congress in the 1790s 
enacted several statutes that appear to give the President or other 
administrators the power to make rules, in the sense of directives deciding 
many individual outcomes on a generic basis. Some examples are:
In 1790, Congress provided that any U.S. soldier “wounded or 
disabled” in service was to receive benefits “at such rate of pay, and 
under such regulations as shall be directed by the President,” limited 
only by the parameters that the ‘Tiighest disability” be capped at half-
pay for officers and $5 per month for others and that lesser 
disabilities be compensated by “a sum in proportion to the highest 
disability.” * * *
